request: A story about a girl named Alice and her best friend Bob, who happens to be a cat.

first_draft.title: Alice and Bob's Missing Jingle
first_draft.text:
Alice lived at the top of a crooked house on Pebble Lane, and her best friend was a ginger cat called Bob. Bob had one white sock on his back left paw and a silver bell that hung from a blue ribbon around his neck. Every morning he trotted into her room, going jingle, jingle, jingle across the floorboards, then leapt onto her quilt with a soft thump.

"Good morning, Bob," said Alice, rubbing her sleepy eyes. Bob pressed his cold nose against hers, which was their special hello, and they both giggled.

One Saturday, Alice woke up and listened. No jingle. She listened again. Only the clock going tick, tock, and a sparrow chirping on the windowsill.

"Bob?" she called. He padded in with his tail held high, but he made no sound at all. The blue ribbon was still there, dangling loose and empty.

"Oh no," said Alice. "Where did your bell go?"

They searched together. Alice looked under the sofa, behind the teapot and inside her wellington boots. Bob searched too, though he mostly sniffed the bread bin and tried to squeeze into the laundry basket. Alice felt a wobble in her tummy. Bob's bell was how she always knew he was near.

They checked the kitchen, the bathroom and the airing cupboard. Alice found a sock, two buttons and a very surprised spider, but no bell. At last she pulled on her yellow raincoat and carried Bob out into the garden. The wet grass sparkled. The apple tree dripped.

"Bob, we have to be super quiet," Alice whispered. "Then we might hear it."

They sat on the old wooden bench. Bob's ears swivelled like tiny radar dishes. A snail slid past. A wood pigeon cooed. Somewhere a tap went plip, plop. Alice held her breath and listened harder.

Then a breeze stirred the lavender, and from somewhere under the bench came a faint, tiny ting.

Bob's whiskers twitched. He wriggled off the seat and flattened himself on the path, nose pressed to a gap between the boards. "Bob, you silly thing," Alice giggled, "is it down there?"

She lay on her tummy, cold and damp, and reached under the bench. The ribbon had slipped loose, and the bell had dropped through a crack. Her fingers brushed something smooth, then something cold and round. She pulled it out. Her silver bell, a little muddy, glinted in her palm.

She gave it a gentle shake. Jingle! Bob leapt up so fast that he bumped her chin, and then he purred like a little motorboat.

Together they sat on the path while Alice tied the ribbon in a double knot. Bob sat so patiently that she almost thought he was a statue. His ears were flat with embarrassment, but he forgave her with one slow blink. Then he butted his head against her wellies, and they walked back inside, jingling all the way.

That evening the rain tapped softly on the window. Alice tucked herself into bed, and Bob curled up on her feet like a warm, furry loaf.

Jingle, went the bell, as he turned one slow circle. Ting. Then the bell went still.

"Goodnight, Bob," Alice whispered. His purr rolled on, low and slow, like a sleepy train far away.

Alice's eyes grew heavy. The rain whispered, the clock said tock, and the house settled in around them. The little bell lay quiet at last.

request: Leo and his dog Rocket go on a treasure hunt in the backyard

first_draft.title: Captain Leo and the Backyard Treasure
first_draft.text:
Leo woke up early on Saturday with a map folded under his pillow. It was a pirate map, dotted with X marks and drawn in brown ink that smelled faintly of toast. Rocket, his scruffy brown dog, was already awake, thumping his tail against the bed. "Today," Leo whispered, "we find the treasure of Captain Bristlebeard."

Out in the backyard, the grass was wet and silver with dew. The old apple tree creaked in the breeze, and a blue jay scolded them from the fence. Leo unrolled the map on the back step. The first clue read: Where the shadow of the shed is longest, dig with a spoon and a prayer.

Rocket sniffed the shed wall, then trotted to the corner where the shadow stretched across the flowerbed. He began to dig, paws flying, dirt spraying like confetti. "Rocket, wait!" Leo laughed, grabbing the trowel. They dug together, scoop by scoop, until the trowel clinked against something hard. It was a tin box with a rusty latch. Inside was a folded note and a chocolate coin wrapped in gold foil.

The second clue was trickier. Climb no ladder, cross no fence, find the place where the wind plays hide and seek. Leo frowned at the map. Rocket sat down, tilted his head, and gave a small, confused whine. Then a gust blew through the garden and rattled the wind chimes by the back door. Leo's eyes lit up. "The chimes! Rocket, the wind is hiding right there!"

Behind the chimes, taped under the porch rail, was a second envelope. Rocket barked so loudly that a sleepy robin flapped out of the hedge. Leo tore open the envelope and read the last clue aloud in his best pirate voice. "Beneath the old wheelbarrow, where the caterpillars nap, lies the greatest treasure of all!"

They raced to the wheelbarrow, tipped it gently on its side, and found a bundle wrapped in a faded blue towel. Inside was a small wooden chest painted with stars. Leo opened it slowly. There were no jewels, only a stack of homemade pirate stickers, a jar of golden honey, and a note in careful handwriting: For the captain and his crew, who found the way together.

Leo grinned and gave Rocket a big hug. Rocket licked his nose, then wagged so hard his whole back end wiggled. "Best treasure ever," Leo said, and Rocket yawned, as if he agreed.

The sun climbed higher and then began to sink. Back in the house, Leo tucked the map beside his bed and the wooden chest on the windowsill. Rocket curled into his blanket at the foot of the bed, one ear twitching. The wind chimes sang softly outside, and the apple tree sighed its leafy sigh.

Leo's eyes grew heavy. The stars came out one by one above the garden, quiet and bright. Somewhere below, a cricket hummed, and the moon slid gently across the sky. Rocket's breathing slowed. Leo pulled up his covers and closed his eyes.

Goodnight, little captain. Goodnight, good dog. The treasure is safe, and so are you.

first_draft.title: Pim and the Big Blue Sky
first_draft.text:
High above the Misty Hills, a little dragon named Pim sat on the edge of her cave. Her scales were the color of warm toast. Her wings were folded tight against her back.

"Up you go, Pim," called her mother from the sky. "The wind is waiting."

Pim shook her head. Her tail curled round her feet. "Not today," she whispered. "The sky is too big."

Her mother landed softly beside her. "Big things can be good things," she said, and she rubbed Pim's nose with her own.

The next morning, Pim tried again. She flapped her wings. Flap, flap, flop. She tumbled down the grassy slope like a rolling pinecone. Bump, bump, bump!

Her friend Barnaby the owl blinked from a branch. "Ouch," he hooted. "Are you hurt?"

"Only my pride," said Pim, and she giggled, even though her cheeks were pink.

Barnaby hopped down beside her. "What if you start small? Flap your wings while your feet stay on the ground."

So Pim tried. Whoosh went her wings. Swish, swish, swish! Dust puffed up around her like a little cloud. Her nose tickled. She sneezed, "Ah-CHOO!" and Barnaby fell off his branch in surprise.

Both of them laughed until their bellies wobbled.

Then Pim noticed something. Her wings felt lighter when she laughed. Her heart felt lighter too.

She stood up tall. She spread her wings wide. She took one long breath, and then another. The wind tickled her scales.

"Ready?" asked Barnaby.

"Ready," said Pim.

She ran. Thump, thump, thump went her feet. She leaped. Whoosh! Up she rose, just a little, just above the grass. Her tail swished behind her like a happy ribbon.

"I'm flying!" she squeaked. "Look, Barnaby, I'm flying!"

Her mother circled above, and her golden eyes shone with pride.

Pim glided over the hills, just a few wing-lengths at a time. She dipped and swooped. She wobbled and steadied. Each time she landed, she felt a little bit braver.

At last, the sun slipped low behind the hills. The sky turned peach, then lavender, then soft blue.

Pim curled up in her cave, her wings tucked snug. Barnaby settled on the rock beside her. Her mother hummed a low, slow song.

Hush, went the wind. Hush, went the leaves.

Pim's eyelids drooped. Her breath grew slow and even.

Tomorrow, the sky would still be big.

But tonight, the dragon was fast asleep.

final.title: Pim and the Big Blue Sky
final.text:
High above the Misty Hills, a little dragon named Pim sat on the edge of her cave. Her scales were the color of warm toast. Her wings were folded tight against her back, and her tail curled round her feet like a sleepy cat.

"Up you go, Pim," called her mother from the sky. "The wind is waiting for you."

Pim shook her head. "Not today," she whispered. "The sky is too big. It goes on and on and on."

Her mother landed softly beside her, with a sound like a rug being shaken out. "The sky is big," she agreed. Then she rubbed Pim's nose with her own. "Try again tomorrow, little one."

The next morning, Pim tried again. She flapped her wings. Flap, flap, flop. She tumbled down the grassy slope like a rolling pinecone. Bump, bump, bump! She landed in a bush with a crunch and a rustle.

Her friend Barnaby the owl blinked from a branch. "Ouch," he hooted. "Are you hurt?"

"Only my pride," said Pim, and she giggled, even though her cheeks were pink. A leaf stuck out of her ear.

Barnaby hopped down beside her and tugged the leaf free. "What if you start small? Flap your wings while your feet stay on the ground."

So Pim tried. Whoosh went her wings. Swish, swish, swish! Dust puffed up around her like a little cloud. Her nose tickled. She sneezed, "Ah-CHOO!" and Barnaby fell off his branch in surprise. Plop!

Both of them laughed until their bellies wobbled. Pim laughed so hard that she hiccuped. "Hic! Hic!" Barnaby hooted every time she did, and that made them laugh even more.

Then Pim noticed something. Her wings felt lighter when she laughed. Her heart felt lighter too.

She stood up tall. She spread her wings wide. She took one long breath, and then another. The wind tickled her scales and smelled of pine and rain.

"Ready?" asked Barnaby.

"Almost," said Pim. She looked down at the grass, far below. Then she looked up at the sky. "Ready."

She ran. Thump, thump, thump went her feet. She leaped. Whoosh! Up she rose, just a little, just above the grass. Her tail swished behind her like a happy ribbon.

"I'm flying!" she squeaked. "Look, Barnaby, I'm flying!"

Barnaby flapped alongside her, hooting with delight. "Hoot-hoot-hooray!"

Her mother circled above, and her golden eyes shone with pride.

Pim glided over the hills, just a few wing-lengths at a time. She dipped and swooped. She wobbled and steadied. Once she bumped into a cloud and came out with a wet nose, and she giggled all the way down. Each time she landed, she felt a little bit braver.

At last, the sun slipped low behind the hills. The sky turned peach, then lavender, then soft blue.

Pim curled up in her cave, her wings tucked snug. Barnaby settled on the rock beside her. Her mother hummed a low, slow song.

Hush, went the wind. Hush, went the leaves.

Pim's eyelids drooped. Her breath grew slow and even.

Tomorrow, the sky would still be big.

But tonight, the dragon was fast asleep.

first_draft.title: The Midnight Party in the Fridge
first_draft.text:
At midnight, when the kitchen clock gave its tired little tick, the fridge door creaked open just a crack. A cold, silvery light spilled across the tiles, and somewhere inside, a tiny trumpet went *toot-a-doo-doo!*

Hector the hedgehog-shaped salt pot woke first. Well, he was not really a hedgehog, but the kitchen mice liked to say so. He peeked out from behind the bread bin with one bleary eye. "Is it morning?" he whispered.

"No, it is PARTY time," squeaked Orla, the mouse with the very long whiskers. She wiggled her nose. "The vegetables are having a secret midnight party, and we are invited!"

But there was a problem. Ferdinand the carrot had been left out of the list. He sat alone on the bottom shelf, his orange cheeks drooping. "Nobody wants a crunchy old carrot," he sighed, and his leaves gave a sad little rustle.

"Nonsense!" boomed a voice from the cheese drawer. It was Bodhi the broccoli, who was very tall and very green and very fond of wobbling when he laughed. "Every party needs a carrot. Who else will do the crunch-crunch dance?"

So the four friends set to work. Orla tiptoed up the shelf, her whiskers twitching, and tugged a sparkly ribbon from a cracker box. Hector rolled a bottle cap across the floor, clink, clink, clink, to make a drum. Bodhi puffed out his florets and went *ffff-ploof!* like a very polite sneeze.

But when they reached the top shelf, they found the party was already going on without them. Peas were bouncing on the butter. A row of cucumbers was doing a wobbly conga line. Nobody had saved a place for Ferdinand.

Hector scratched his salty head. "A party needs a special place," he said slowly. "A place just for the guest of honour."

So Orla fetched the ribbon. Hector fetched the bottle cap. Bodhi lowered his tall green self down like a bridge, and Ferdinand scrambled up his leafy stem. Together they built a throne out of the lid of a yogurt pot, decorated with peas and a single shiny grape.

"Ladies and gentlemen," announced Bodhi, "our crunchiest guest, Ferdinand the Carrot!"

The whole fridge cheered. The cucumbers stopped their conga line to clap. Ferdinand's leaves stood up tall and proud, and he did the crunch-crunch dance so loudly that the milk jug giggled and sloshed.

At last the party began to quiet. The music of the bottle-cap drum grew softer. Orla's whiskers drooped. Bodhi folded his florets in a sleepy bundle. Hector yawned a yawn as wide as a biscuit tin.

"Shh," whispered Ferdinand, tucking a leaf under his chin. "Listen."

The fridge hummed its gentle hum. A drip of water fell, plip, into the crisper drawer. Somewhere far away, a clock ticked, tick, tock, tick.

One by one, the friends curled up in the cool, quiet light. The party lanterns dimmed to a glow. The mice slipped back to their hole. The door swung softly closed, click.

And in the dark, a small orange carrot dreamed of crunchy dances, while the fridge hummed its lullaby, hush, hush, goodnight.

first_draft.title: Oona and the Wandering Button
first_draft.text:
The lighthouse keeper's cat, Mabel, had a habit of hiding things. Her favorite hiding place was the long brass telescope on the windowsill, and that was where Oona found the small blue button on Thursday evening.

"A button!" whispered Oona, holding it up to the lamp. It was round and cold, with a tiny anchor carved on its face. "Whose button could this be?"

Mabel blinked slowly and said nothing at all, which was not very helpful.

Downstairs, Grandpa Hector was humming while he polished the great glass lens. Every night he said the same thing: "A lighthouse needs all its pieces, Oona, or it can't tell the sailors where the rocks are." Oona had never thought about it much until now. Somewhere, a coat was missing a button, and a sailor might be buttoning it up in the dark.

She tucked the button into her pocket and went looking. She checked the kitchen drawer, where the spoons jingled like tiny bells. She checked the woolly blanket on the armchair, and the basket of socks by the stove. She found a bent paperclip, two marbles, and a fish-shaped eraser, but no coat.

"Mabel," said Oona, sitting on the bottom step, "you have to help me. Where did you find it?"

Mabel stretched, yawned, and padded up the stairs. Oona followed, her slippers going pit-pat, pit-pat on each step, until they reached the little round room at the top of the tower. There, hanging on a hook beside the door, was an old yellow raincoat. One of its buttons was missing. The empty threads were there, just waiting.

Oona's heart gave a happy skip. She held the blue button against the gap. It fit perfectly.

"Grandpa," she called down the stairwell, "I found it!"

Hector climbed up slowly, one hand on the rail, his knees creaking like an old rowboat. When he saw the coat, he laughed so hard his spectacles slid down his nose. "Well, would you look at that. Our wandering button came home."

Together they sewed it on, Oona holding the thread steady while Grandpa pushed the needle through. It took three tries. The first try went into Oona's thumb, which made her giggle, and the second bent the needle into a sad little hook. The third time, the button sat snug and neat.

That night, the lamp turned slowly above them, sending its gold beam across the dark sea, and the yellow coat hung still and proud on its hook.

Oona climbed into bed. The sheets smelled of lavender and sunshine. Outside, the waves whispered against the rocks, hush and hush, hush and hush.

Grandpa tucked the blanket under her chin. "Goodnight, little keeper."

"Goodnight, Grandpa," she murmured. Mabel curled up at her feet, purring like a tiny engine.

The lamp turned, and turned, and the sea kept its soft song, and the little blue button sat quietly in its place, keeping watch until morning.

first_draft.title: Ferdinand and the Very Sleepy Hen
first_draft.text:
On Clover Farm, a goat named Ferdinand woke up with a problem. His bell was gone. Every morning it went clang, clang, clang. Without it, nobody knew when to start the day.

“Where is my bell?” he bleated. “Maa-ooh! Has anyone seen it?”

The sheep just chewed their grass. The ducks went quack, quack, quack. Imogen the pig snorted, “Did you look in the mud?” Ferdinand did not want to look in the mud.

Ferdinand trotted into the barn. Something round sat in the straw. A hen named Wren was sitting on it, her feathers puffed up like a pillow. “Shh,” she whispered. “I am hatching an egg.” Ferdinand peeked. A tiny shiny corner poked out from under her wing. It was his bell!

“Wren,” said Ferdinand, “that is not an egg. That is my bell.”

Wren blinked her round eyes. “Oh my. It is very smooth. And very cold. I thought it was a big, sleepy egg.” She stood up. The bell rolled out of the straw. Ding! Wren jumped straight up in the air. “Cluck! The egg rang!”

Ferdinand tried being quiet, the way Wren liked. He sat down in the straw. He waited. Wren wiggled. She fluffed. She made a squeaky noise, like a door that needed oil. “Cluck-a-doodle-oink!” Imogen the pig passed by, giggled so hard she snorted bubbles.

Then Wren yawned a huge yawn. “Well,” she said, “I suppose I am not hatching anything today.” She hopped out into the sunshine. Ferdinand picked up his bell and gave it a polite little shake. Ding. Wren clapped her wings. “Wonderful! Ring it again!”

The sun slid down behind the hill. The hens tucked their heads under their wings. The ducks stopped quacking. Imogen snored, soft as a bellows. Ferdinand’s bell hung quiet on its hook. Tonight, nobody needed to ring it.

Ferdinand closed his eyes. Goodnight, Clover Farm. Goodnight, Wren. Goodnight, bell.

first_draft.title: Cleo and the Sock-Loving Monster
first_draft.text:
Cleo heard a crunch under her bed. Crunch, crunch, munch. She peeked over the edge of her blanket, and two big yellow eyes blinked back at her, shiny as wet pebbles. "Good evening," said a voice like warm bubbles. "I am Oswin. I am a monster, but please do not be alarmed. I only eat socks."

Cleo looked down at him. He was round and fuzzy, the color of oatmeal, with ears like two floppy teapot lids. In one paw he held a striped sock, and his whiskers were full of lint. "Those are my socks," Cleo said, sitting up. "All of them?" "Only the ones that smell of adventure," Oswin said, and he sniffed the sock with great delight. "Mmm. Muddy garden, with a hint of toast."

Cleo wiggled her bare toes. Her drawer was nearly empty, and tomorrow was Monday. "Oswin, I have one pair left, and school is in the morning." His ears drooped like wet paper. "Monsters must eat something," he sighed. "What do you like besides socks?" Oswin thought so hard that his nose wrinkled. "Pancakes," he whispered at last. "Fat, golden ones, with a puddle of syrup. But I have never had one. Monsters are not allowed near the kitchen."

Cleo grinned. She had an idea, but she knew better than to reach for the stove alone. She tiptoed downstairs, where Dad was reading by the fire with his feet up. "A monster who likes pancakes?" Dad said, yawning. "Well, I make a very good pancake. You can stir."

Together they mixed flour, eggs and milk in a big yellow bowl. Cleo stirred so hard that a puff of flour floated up like a little cloud. Dad flipped each pancake with a sizzle and a pop. When the stack was tall and warm, Cleo carried the plate upstairs, one careful step at a time. Oswin's nose twitched. "Oh," he breathed. "Oh my." He ate one, then another, humming tiny happy hums that sounded like a kettle starting to boil.

When the plate was empty, Oswin patted his round tummy. It gurgled like a bathtub draining. Then he looked guilty. "I have a confession," he whispered. He pushed a fuzzy paw under the bed and pulled out a heap of socks. There were red ones, spotty ones, and one with a hole where a toe used to be. "I was keeping them warm," he said. "Every sock needs a cozy place to sleep."

Cleo counted eleven socks and one tiny sock shaped like a bear. "You can keep the bear one," she said, "because you hugged it best." Oswin's yellow eyes shone. "Pancakes on Tuesdays?" he asked hopefully. Cleo giggled. "Pancakes on Tuesdays. With Dad."

Dad carried the sock pile downstairs and set it by the washing machine. Cleo pulled on a pair of striped socks, warm and dry, and climbed into bed. Oswin curled up under the bed, one crumb of pancake stuck to his chin.

The clock ticked softly. The house went quiet. Outside, the moon sat low over the garden like a silver plate.

"Goodnight, Oswin," Cleo whispered.

"Goodnight, Cleo," rumbled the monster, softer and softer, like a kettle cooling down.

Shh. Sleep now.

first_draft.text:
The old house at the end of Heron Lane had a voice. When the wind leaned on the windows, the floorboards creaked, and somewhere high above the stairs something went whoo-oo, whoo-oo, like a sigh with a cold.

Osric pulled his blanket up to his nose. "That's a ghost," he whispered.

Bea sat up in the trundle bed. Moonlight lay across the rug in silver stripes. "Ghosts don't have colds," she said. "Let's find out."

They crept along the landing in their socks. The third stair went eeek. The fourth went eeeeek, and Osric clapped a hand over his mouth. Shadows stretched across the wallpaper like long, thin fingers.

The whoo-oo grew louder as they climbed toward the attic. The door stood open a crack, and a cold breeze slipped out, smelling of dusty books and peppermints.

Inside, a rocking chair was rocking all by itself. Creak, creak, creak. Then a wobbly voice said, "Oh, goodness me. Visitors! Do mind the trunk, dears. It squeaks when you sit on it."

The chair stopped. Floating a foot above the floorboards was a small ghost in a lace nightcap, her spectacles slipping down her nose. Her smile was kind.

"I'm dreadfully sorry I frightened you. I'm Opal Thistlewood. I used to hum this whole house to sleep, but I've lost the key to my music box, and without it my humming has gone all wheezy. Hence the noise."

"Hence the noise," Osric repeated, and some of the stiffness left his shoulders.

"Where did you last see it?" asked Bea.

"It slipped through my fingers and fell down a crack by the chimney," Opal said.

Osric knelt and peered into the gap. All he could see was darkness and a faint smell of cheese. Bea pulled a hairpin from her hair. "Hold the lamp steady," she said.

She wiggled the pin into the gap. Something tugged back. "It's stuck," she whispered. "Or it's alive!"

A small brown mouse popped out, a ball of pink wool in its paws, the silver key dangling from the middle like a fish on a hook. Its whiskers twitched. Its nose wrinkled. "Ah-CHOO!"

Osric laughed so hard he nearly dropped the lamp. Opal's shoulders shook, and a sound like tinkling bells drifted out of her. "That's Mr. Crumb," she said. "He collects anything shiny and anything soft."

Bea coaxed the key free. Mr. Crumb sneezed once more, then scampered off, chirping crossly.

Opal lifted the lid of a little wooden music box on the sill and set the key in place. She turned it. Tink, tink, tink went a tune, slow and sweet. She began to hum along.

The house listened. The floorboards stopped creaking. The wind slid down the chimney and softened into a sigh that matched the tune. Whoo-oo, it sang, now like a lullaby.

"Oh, that's much better. Thank you, both of you." Opal pulled two patchwork quilts from the trunk, smelling of lavender, and floated them down the stairs. "Now, off to bed. Mustn't keep the house awake."

On the landing, the stairs were silent. The shadows had shrunk back into the corners, small and sleepy, and the moon hung low over the rooftops like a lamp left on for them.

Bea tucked herself under her quilt by the window. Osric pulled his up to his chin and let out a long, slow yawn.

Below, the kettle ticked as it cooled. Above, the music box played one last small note, and then the house was quiet.

"Goodnight, Opal," Bea whispered.

From the attic, faint as a feather, came the reply. "Goodnight, dears. Sleep well."

first_draft.title: Sir Dorian and the Goose Who Borrowed Luck
first_draft.text:
The morning smelled of cut grass and warm pears when Sir Dorian polished his helmet until it shone like a spoon. Across the lawn, Sir Lorcan swung his practice sword in long, whistling loops. Whoosh. Whoosh. Whoosh.

"Are you ready, Sir Dorian?" called Lorcan, grinning beneath a tall plume of green feathers.

"Ready as a rooster at sunrise," replied Dorian. He lifted his wooden sword. It had a crack down the middle and a splash of blue paint on the handle. It was not the shiniest sword in the kingdom, but it was his.

The rules were simple. Two knights, one ring of white pebbles, and the first to tap the other's shield three times would win the Silver Spoon, a silly trophy the Queen kept on her windowsill.

Then Dorian reached into his pocket for his lucky whetstone, the smooth grey stone he rubbed before every contest. His fingers found only crumbs.

"Lorcan," he said slowly, "where is my whetstone?"

Lorcan's grin wobbled. "I haven't touched it! Honestly, Dorian."

"You stared at it all through breakfast," said Dorian, and his cheeks turned as pink as strawberry jam.

Noor, the gardener's daughter, sat on the wall with a basket of runner beans. She tilted her head. "Maybe it wasn't a knight at all," she said. "Listen."

From the hedge came a loud, proud honk. Out waddled a big white goose named Mabel, with a bit of ribbon tangled around one foot. Mabel was famous in the castle for stealing shiny things: spoons, buttons, and once, a bell from the chapel.

"Mabel," said Dorian, and his voice was half cross and half amused, "you have been borrowing my luck."

Mabel hissed and flapped her wings, scattering pebbles across the lawn. Dorian did not charge at her, and he did not shout. He knelt down slowly, the way you would approach a sleepy cat, and held out a crisp lettuce leaf.

"Would you like to trade?" he whispered.

Mabel eyed the leaf. She eyed the knight. Then, with a sniff, she tipped her head and let the grey stone roll out from under her wing. She took the lettuce in one crunchy bite.

Lorcan laughed so hard he had to sit down on the grass. "Who knew a goose could out-sneak a knight?"

"Who knew a knight could be so polite to a goose?" said Dorian, and he offered Lorcan his hand, a little sheepishly.

They took their places in the ring. Dorian rubbed the whetstone three times for luck. It felt warm and smooth between his fingers. Lorcan danced left. Dorian spun right. Wooden swords clacked and clattered, tap and tap and tap.

At the very same moment, each knight tapped the other's shield for the third time.

"A tie!" declared Noor, clapping her hands from the top of the wall.

Lorcan pretended to frown. "Next time I'll win, Sir Dorian."

"Next time you'll have to find your own goose," said Dorian, and they both giggled.

The Queen arrived with a tray of warm honey buns and handed the Silver Spoon to the two knights to share. They passed it back and forth, polishing it on their sleeves until it gleamed like a little moon. Mabel waddled over, snatched a bun from Lorcan's plate, and honked as if she had won the whole contest.

The sun slipped down behind the castle towers. The lawn turned soft and blue. Dorian tucked the whetstone into his pocket, still warm from the afternoon. Lorcan's plume drooped in the evening breeze. Somewhere in the hedge, Mabel settled with a sleepy sigh.

Noor folded her basket and walked home along the garden path, her footsteps quiet on the stones.

Dorian yawned. The lanterns flickered once, then glowed steady and low.

"Goodnight, Mabel," he whispered. "Goodnight, lucky stone."

first_draft.title: Maya and the Whale Family
first_draft.text:
Maya's new shoes squeaked on the hallway floor. Squeak, squeak, squeak. Her tummy felt wobbly, like jelly on a plate.

On Sunday night, Mum sat on the edge of her bed. "New places can feel big," she said. "That wobbly feeling is normal."

Maya hugged her bear, Biscuit. "What if nobody wants to be my friend?" Biscuit's stitched smile did not change. He never worried about anything.

On Monday, the classroom buzzed like a beehive. Children sat in bunches, laughing and swapping stickers. Maya stood by the coat hooks, holding her lunchbox with both hands.

"Maya, you can sit by the window, next to the plant," said Ms. Delphine. Maya walked slowly. Squeak. Squeak.

The plant had three leaves that curled like tiny hands. Maya touched one gently. It felt soft, like velvet.

At lunchtime, Maya carried her tray to the bench outside. The sun was warm. A breeze tickled her ears.

Across the yard, a boy named Thaddeus hopped like a frog. "Ribbit! Ribbit! Splat!" He landed in a puddle, and his socks went squish, squish.

Some children laughed. Maya giggled behind her hand. Then she wanted to join them, but her feet felt stuck to the bench.

She opened her mouth. Nothing came out. She took a bite of cheese cracker instead. Crunch. Crunch. Crunch.

At the far end of the bench sat a girl named Yara. She was drawing with a purple crayon. Swish, swish, swish.

Maya peeked over. "Is that a whale?" she asked quietly.

"It's a whale with a kite tail," Yara said. "It flies when the wind blows."

Maya opened her pencil case. On the lid was a whale too, with a dotted belly. "Mine has spots," she said. Yara's eyes lit up.

Soon they were drawing a whole whale family. Yara made a baby whale. Maya made a big one with a bow on its head.

Ribbit! Splat! Thaddeus landed right beside them, dripping. "Can I draw a frog whale?" he asked.

"Yes," said Maya. "A very wet one." Everyone giggled.

Then a girl named Inigo came over with a sketchbook full of rockets. "Rockets can fly to the whale's moon," she said. So they did.

The bell rang. Ding, ding, ding. Maya's tummy still wobbled a little, but less than before.

In line, Yara stood behind her. "See you tomorrow, Whale Girl?"

Maya grinned. "See you tomorrow," she said. Her sneakers went squeak, squeak, and they sounded happy.

At home, Maya showed Mum the drawing. The whale family was crowded onto the page, with a frog, two rockets, and one soggy sock.

Mum tapped the paper. "Who drew all this?"

"Me and some new friends," Maya said. She liked how the words sounded.

Night came slowly. The hallway light dimmed to gold. The house grew quiet.

Squeak, went the bed springs as Maya snuggled down. Then softer. Squeak. Squeak.

Biscuit sat on her pillow, whiskers still. Maya yawned a big yawn, the kind that makes your eyes water.

Hush, said the wind outside. Hush, said the tree. Maya's eyes closed, one heavy blink at a time.

"Goodnight, little whales," Maya whispered. "Goodnight."

first_draft.title: Sam and the Hedgehog Under the Apple Tree
first_draft.text:
Sam lay in bed with one sock on and one sock off, listening to the house settle for the night. The fridge hummed. The pipes clicked and ticked. Downstairs, a spoon tapped against a mug, tink, tink, tink. But the rug beside his bed was empty, and that was the quietest sound of all.

Biscuit had slept on that rug for nine years. He had one floppy ear, a tail that wagged like a windscreen wiper, and a snore that sounded like a kettle waking up. Last week Biscuit died, on the warm grass in the garden, with Sam's hand resting on his back. Sam still did not know what to do with the feeling in his chest. Sometimes it felt heavy, like a stone in a pocket. Sometimes it felt like a sneeze that would not come.

Mum came in with a glass of water and sat on the edge of the bed. "I keep forgetting," Sam said. "I go to the kitchen and look for his bowl. Then I remember."

Mum nodded and stroked his hair. "Me too, love. Every morning I reach for his lead by the door."

Sam pulled his blanket up to his chin. "I wish I could tell him things. Like how I finally learned to whistle."

"Maybe we can find a way," Mum said softly.

The next morning, Sam found Biscuit's squeaky hedgehog wedged under the sofa. It was flat and grey, and it had only one eye left. Sam squeezed it, and it gave a small, sad squeak. "Eek."

He knew exactly where it belonged. Under the apple tree, where the grass was soft and the bees hummed lazily, was Biscuit's favourite spot for napping. Sam wanted a stone there, a flat one with his dog's name painted on it, so the hedgehog would have a proper home.

Dad found a big grey stone by the fence. "Too heavy for you, Sam," he said.

"I can do it," Sam puffed. He tried to lift it, but it only wobbled in his arms. Then he tried to roll it, and it bumped over a dandelion and stopped.

Dad fetched the red wheelbarrow. It squeaked with every push, eeek, eeek, eeek, just like the hedgehog. Sam giggled, even though his eyes were wet. "It sounds like Biscuit is still complaining about the bath," he said.

Dad laughed. "Steer it with me, Sam."

Together they rolled the stone across the lawn, one slow bump at a time. They dug a small hole beneath the apple tree. Sam placed the hedgehog inside, right where the shade was deepest.

Then he took a breath. "You chased the hose until you got soaked," he said. "You ate one whole sock. You snored louder than the car."

Dad sat down on the grass beside him. "He once stole a whole sausage off my plate at a barbecue," Dad said. "I was so cross. Now I miss that sneaky face."

Sam laughed, and then he cried a little, and then he laughed again. Dad put an arm around him, and neither of them hurried.

That night, Sam lay in bed again, with both socks off and his toes wiggling under the blanket. The house was quiet. The fridge hummed softly. Outside, the apple tree rustled its leaves.

He thought about the rug, and he thought about the stone under the tree. The rug was still empty, but it did not feel quite so empty now.

"Goodnight, Biscuit," Sam whispered. The room stayed calm and still, and his eyes slowly closed.

first_draft.title: Thaddeus and the Missing Blanket
first_draft.text:
High in an old oak tree, where the moon hung like a silver lamp, lived a sleepy owl named Thaddeus.

His feathers were soft and gray. His eyes were heavy, heavy, heavy.

"Hoo, hoo," he yawned. "Time for bed."

He tucked his head under one wing and settled into his nest. Then he felt a cold draft. The blanket was gone.

It was his favorite blanket, a warm square of soft wool. Thaddeus peeked over the branch. Far below, the blanket fluttered on a fence post like a tiny flag.

"Oh, hoo," he sighed. "I cannot sleep without it."

He glided down, soft as a feather, and tugged at the wool with his beak. It would not budge.

Then a rustle came from the grass. A field mouse named Bramble poked out her whiskers.

"Hello, sleepy owl," she squeaked. "Why are you so grumpy?"

"My blanket is stuck," said Thaddeus. "Hoo, hoo, what shall I do?"

Bramble scurried up the post. She sniffed. She wiggled. Her nose twitched with care. She found a loop of wool caught on a nail.

"Pull with me," she said. "One, two, three!"

They tugged. Tug, tug, tug. Pop! The blanket came loose and floated down into Thaddeus's talons.

"Thank you, Bramble," he said with a soft smile.

"Hoo-hoo, you are welcome," Bramble said. "Now go to sleep."

Thaddeus flapped back up to his nest, shook out the blanket, and wrapped it snugly around his shoulders. Bramble waved her tiny paw from the fence. "Goodnight, Thaddeus!"

Hoo, hoo, the night is still. Hoo, hoo, the moon is high.

The wind hummed softly through the leaves. Somewhere, a cricket sang a sleepy song. Down in the grass, Bramble tucked herself into a bed of clover.

Thaddeus let his eyes drift closed. His feathers puffed. His breath grew slow.

Hoo... hush... the moon is near. Hoo... hush... goodnight, dear.

final.title: Thaddeus and the Missing Blanket
final.text:
High in an old oak tree, where the moon hung like a silver lamp, lived a sleepy owl named Thaddeus.

His feathers were soft and gray. His eyes were heavy, heavy, heavy.

"Hoo, hoo," he yawned. "Time for bed."

He tucked his head under one wing and settled into his nest. Then he felt a cold draft. The blanket was gone.

It was his favorite blanket, a warm square of soft wool. Thaddeus peeked over the branch. Far below, the blanket fluttered on a fence post like a tiny flag.

"Oh, hoo," he sighed. "I cannot sleep without it."

He glided down, soft as a feather, and tugged at the wool with his beak. It would not budge.

Then a rustle came from the grass. A field mouse named Bramble poked out her whiskers.

"Hello, sleepy owl," she squeaked. "Why are you so grumpy?"

"My blanket is stuck," said Thaddeus. "Hoo, hoo, what shall I do?"

Bramble scurried up the post. She sniffed. She wiggled. Her nose twitched with care. She found a loop of wool caught on a nail.

"Pull with me," she said. "One, two, three!"

They tugged. Tug, tug, tug. Pop! The blanket came loose and floated down into Thaddeus's talons.

"Thank you, Bramble," he said with a soft smile.

"Hoo-hoo, you are welcome," Bramble said. "Now go to sleep."

Thaddeus flapped back up to his nest, shook out the blanket, and wrapped it snugly around his shoulders. Bramble waved her tiny paw from the fence. "Goodnight, Thaddeus!"

Hoo, hoo, the night is still. Hoo, hoo, the moon is high.

The wind hummed softly through the leaves. Somewhere, a cricket sang a sleepy song. Down in the grass, Bramble tucked herself into a bed of clover.

Thaddeus let his eyes drift closed. His feathers puffed. His breath grew slow.

Hoo... hush... the moon is near. Hoo... hush... goodnight, dear.

first_draft.title: Zoe and the Crystal Cave
first_draft.text:
On the last warm afternoon of summer, Zoe climbed the green hill behind her grandma's farm with her tortoise, Pebble, trundling along beside her. Pebble walked the way he did everything, one slow step at a time, his shell gleaming like a polished chestnut. Zoe was seven and never walked when she could skip, so she kept running ahead, then turning back to wait for him.

Near the top, a crack in the grey rock opened into a dark mouth. A cool breeze drifted out of it, smelling of wet stone and something sweet, like rain on a flower. Zoe knelt down and peered inside. "Pebble, look. A cave!"

Pebble stretched his neck toward the opening, sniffed twice, and then, to Zoe's surprise, went straight in. "Pebble, wait!" She dropped her backpack, pulled out her little flashlight, and clicked it on. The beam danced across walls speckled with glittering dots. "Pebble!" Her voice bounced back at her, softer and softer, until it sounded like someone calling from very far away.

She followed a trail of tiny scratches in the dust, the marks Pebble always left as he walked. The passage was narrow at first, then opened into a wide round room. Zoe stopped, and her breath caught in her throat. Crystals grew out of every wall, pale pink and sky blue and a deep, glowing violet, like a garden frozen in the middle of blooming. When she tapped one gently with her fingernail, it rang like a tiny bell.

"Oh," she breathed. "Crystals. My favorite." Then she heard a soft clink, clink, clink. Pebble stood beside a shallow pool, dipping his nose in the water as calmly as if he were at a picnic. Zoe giggled, and the giggle rolled around the room in a shower of echoes.

Then came a new sound, a low rumble, and a trickle of pebbles tumbling from the ceiling. Dust drifted through the flashlight beam. When it cleared, a heap of rocks blocked the way they had come in. Zoe's heart thumped like a drum. "It's okay," she told herself. "Rocks can be moved. Let's think."

She sat down with Pebble and held very still. Across the room, the breeze was still blowing, cool and steady, against her cheek. "Air comes from somewhere," she whispered. "Pebble, we just have to follow it." She crept along the far wall, past rows of glowing purple crystals, until she found a low, wide tunnel near the floor. It was a squeeze, but the breeze was pouring through it, and at the far end, a thin line of gold light shone through.

Before leaving, Zoe spotted a small pink crystal lying on the floor, sparkling like sugar. She picked it up. It felt warm, as if it had been sitting in the sunshine. She thought about her shelf at home, and how it would look lovely there, next to her other stones. Then she looked back at the great garden of crystals humming quietly in the dark. They had been growing here for a very long time, and they would be just as beautiful tomorrow, and the day after, with nobody holding them. Zoe knelt and set the pink crystal gently beside the pool. "You belong here," she whispered. "Stay and shine for the next visitor."

Pebble climbed into her arms, grumbling a little about being carried, and they wriggled through the tunnel together. On the other side, the hill was bathed in orange light. "Zoe!" a voice called. It was Dad, running up the path with his hair windblown and his face white with worry. Zoe ran to him, dusty and grinning, with Pebble tucked under one arm. He hugged her so tightly that Pebble's head popped out in protest.

"You gave me a fright," Dad said, kneeling down to look at her. "Tell me everything." So Zoe did, from the breeze to the bell-ringing crystals to the rockfall, and Dad listened the whole way through. "You kept your head," he said. "And you kept the crystal where it belonged. That was a kind thing to do."

"I want to tell everyone about the cave," Zoe said, "so they know it's there. But I don't want anyone to take the crystals." Dad smiled and ruffled her hair. "The most wonderful things are best kept safe where they are, Zoe. Then everyone can enjoy them, even the people who come after us."

That night, Pebble snuggled into his cozy box by the window, his shell warm from the day. Zoe lay in bed, listening to the owl calling softly across the fields. Her thoughts drifted back to the violet glow in the cave, the bell-like ring, and the little pink crystal resting by the pool. The moon rose slowly over the hill, and the room grew quiet and silver.

"Goodnight, crystals," Zoe murmured, her eyes growing heavy. "Goodnight, Pebble." Outside, the breeze sighed through the grass, and the hill settled into sleep.
